name: John Locke
summary: Locke argued that government rests on consent to protect life, liberty and property, that legislative and executive powers should be separate, that subjects may resist a government that turns to arbitrary power, and that the magistrate has no authority over souls.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: The Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, drafted with Locke as secretary, set up hereditary landgraves and caciques and made the Lords Proprietors' estates descend to heirs male; the drafting was Shaftesbury's, and Locke's part is not separable.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Held that a church is 'a free and voluntary society. Nobody is born a member of any church', and that no man is by nature bound to any particular church or sect.

ban-interest.rationale: Wrote that money has a 'natural interest' and that when the law sets the rate below it the lender will lend 'at the legal interest' to the banker rather than to tradesmen, so that the lower legal rate harms trade; he accepted a legal maximum rate but not a ban on lending at interest.

character-from-environment.rationale: Wrote in Some Thoughts Concerning Education that 'of all the men we meet with, nine parts of ten are what they are, good or evil, useful or not, by their education', and in the Essay that the mind receives its principles like white paper.

clerical-rule.rationale: Wrote that 'the decisions of churchmen, whose differences and disputes are sufficiently known, cannot be any sounder or safer' than the prince's, and that their suffrages add no strength to the civil power.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Held that men are 'by nature, all free, equal, and independent', so that 'no one can be put out of this estate, and subjected to the political power of another, without his own consent'.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The 1670 Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, drafted with Locke as secretary, make each Lord Proprietor's office descend to his heirs male, then to the next heir general; the drafting was Shaftesbury's and Locke's part is not separable.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: The 1670 Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina, drafted with Locke as secretary, provide in art. 110 that 'Every Freeman of Carolina shall have absolute Power and Authority over his Negro Slaves, of what Opinion or Religion soever' (art. 107 lets slaves join churches but leaves their master's 'civil dominion' unchanged); his own authorship of the clause is not separable from Shaftesbury's, so the answer is low.

filial-duty.rationale: Wrote that children owe parents 'a perpetual obligation of honouring their parents', a 'perpetual right to respect, reverence, support and compliance', which 'ends not with minority, but holds in all parts and conditions of a man's life'.

harm-principle.rationale: Wrote that the commonwealth is 'a society of men constituted only for the procuring, preserving, and advancing their own civil interests', which he called 'life, liberty, health, and indolency of body', and limited the magistrate to punishing violations of them.

money-backed-by-precious-metals.rationale: Wrote in 1695 that 'Silver is the instrument and measure of commerce in all the civilized and trading parts of the world... by its intrinsic value', and opposed raising the nominal value of the coin.

national-self-determination.rationale: Wrote that the descendants of a conquered people 'have always a right to shake it off, and free themselves... till their rulers put them under such a frame of government as they willingly and of choice consent to', citing the Greeks under Turkish rule.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Wrote in the First Treatise that 'Charity gives every Man a Title to so much out of another's Plenty, as will keep him from extream want, where he has no means to subsist otherwise', and that God requires men to afford relief to the wants of their brethren.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Wrote that 'absolute arbitrary power, or governing without settled standing laws' cannot consist with the ends of government, which men enter 'by stated rules of right and property to secure their peace and quiet'.

property-fundamental.rationale: Wrote that 'the supreme power cannot take from any man any part of his property without his own consent: for the preservation of property being the end of government', and that men enter society for 'the preservation of their property'.

reason-over-faith.rationale: In the Essay he wrote that 'faith can never convince us of anything that contradicts our knowledge' and that it is vain to urge as matters of faith propositions contrary to clear perception.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Wrote that when legislators 'take away, and destroy the property of the people, or... reduce them to slavery under arbitrary power, they put themselves into a state of war with the people, who are thereupon absolved from any farther obedience'; the people 'have a right to resume their original liberty'.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Argued that 'the understanding cannot be compelled to the belief of any thing by outward force: confiscation of estate, imprisonment, torments, nothing of that nature can have any such efficacy' to change inward judgment.

self-ownership.rationale: Wrote that 'every man has a property in his own person: this no body has any right to but himself. The labour of his body, and the work of his hands, we may say, are properly his.'

separate-church-state.rationale: Argued that 'all the power of civil government relates only to men's civil interests... and hath nothing to do with the world to come', and that the care of souls is not committed to the civil magistrate.

separated-powers.rationale: Argued that it 'may be too great a temptation to human frailty... for the same persons, who have the power of making laws, to have also in their hands the power to execute them', and so the legislative and executive should be in different hands.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Wrote that husband and wife 'having different understandings, will unavoidably sometimes have different wills', so that 'the last determination, i.e. the rule... naturally falls to the man's share, as the abler and the stronger', in matters of common interest, though without power over her life.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Wrote that men could not have intended 'to give to any one, or more, an absolute arbitrary power over their persons and estates', and that absolute monarchy 'is indeed inconsistent with civil society, and so can be no form of civil-government at all'.

state-harmful.rationale: Wrote that 'civil government is the proper remedy for the inconveniencies of the state of nature', which 'must certainly be great, where men may be judges in their own case'.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Defined a church as 'a voluntary society of men, joining themselves together of their own accord' for worship, denying the magistrate authority over it.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Wrote that nature 'appoints the descent of their Property to their Children, who thus come to have a Title, and natural Right of Inheritance to their Fathers Goods, which the rest of Mankind cannot pretend to'.

taxation-theft.rationale: Wrote that government needs funding and 'it is fit every one who enjoys his share of the protection, should pay out of his estate his proportion for the maintenance of it', but only with consent of the majority or its representatives.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Held that conquest gives no title to land: 'the first conqueror never having had a title to the land of that country', its people may 'shake off the usurpation or tyranny which the sword hath brought in'.

trade-surplus.rationale: Argued in 1691 that a kingdom importing more than it exports loses its money and 'grows doubly poor': if we import 'one hundred thousand pounds worth of commodities, more than we export', our money 'must go out every year' by 'their over-balance of trade', while borrowing from foreigners enriches the kingdom only by 'the over-balance of our exportation to our importation'.

notes: Read by theme: the Second Treatise (Gutenberg 7370), the First Treatise (1698 edition), the 1691 and 1695 money tracts (Works, vol. IV, 1823), The Reasonableness of Christianity (Works vol. VI; searched by theme, no statement answered), the Letter Concerning Toleration, Some Thoughts Concerning Education, the Essay (vol. 1 Book I, vol. 2 Book IV chapter 18) and the 1670 Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina. Thirty-two statements answered, all high or medium except the Carolina act (his authorship is contested). Locke's own text excludes atheists and those owing allegiance to a foreign prince from toleration; no bank statement asks about that.
